source: US Energy Information Administration (EIA), World Oil Transit Chokepoints and Today in Energy notes (2023–2025 flows). Approximate figures; an editor must check them before launch.

items.name: Strait of Hormuz
items.flow: About 20 million barrels of oil a day (2024), roughly a fifth of world oil use, plus about a fifth of world LNG trade.
why: No other route can carry most of the Gulf's oil and gas exports.
Asian buyers such as China, India, Japan and South Korea depend on it most.
Tension with Iran quickly raises world oil prices.

items.name: Strait of Malacca
items.flow: About 23 million barrels of oil a day (2024), the largest oil flow of any chokepoint.
why: The shortest sea route between the Indian Ocean and East Asia.
Most oil bound for China, Japan and South Korea passes through it.
At its narrowest it is under 3 km wide (the Phillips Channel near Singapore).

items.name: Suez Canal
items.flow: About 4–5 million barrels of oil a day in 2024, around half of 2023 levels after attacks on Red Sea shipping.
why: The shortest route between Europe and Asia.
Canal fees are a major source of foreign currency for Egypt.
When ships avoid it they sail around Africa, adding 10 days or more.

items.name: Bab-el-Mandeb
items.flow: About 4 million barrels of oil a day in 2024, down from about 9 million in 2023.
why: The southern gate of the Red Sea, between Yemen and Djibouti.
Houthi attacks on ships since late 2023 cut traffic sharply.
Its closure diverts trade around the Cape of Good Hope.

items.name: Turkish Straits (Bosporus)
items.flow: About 3 million barrels of oil a day, mostly from Russia and the Caspian region.
why: The only sea link between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean.
Türkiye controls passage of warships under the 1936 Montreux Convention.
Ukraine's and Russia's grain exports also pass through it.

items.name: Panama Canal
items.flow: Around 1–2 million barrels of oil and fuel a day, plus US LNG shipped to Asia.
why: Links the Atlantic and Pacific without the long trip around South America.
Droughts in 2023–24 lowered water levels and limited ship crossings.
About two-thirds of its traffic goes to or from the United States.
